source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making
finding: Gives a small formal model of data-frame theory for decisions. Evidence E_t is extracted from raw info, a retrieval function picks a hypothesis (frame) set, a scoring function rates each hypothesis against the evidence. If the best score is under a threshold tau, the next step either extracts more evidence, retrieves more hypotheses, or both.
numbers: Three functions (extract, retrieve, score) and one stopping rule: max score >= tau. Prototype is a skin-cancer tool on the derm7pt dataset with seven concept labels. No user study yet.
quote: if the highest-scoring hypothesis does not meet or exceed an acceptance threshold
limits: Position paper plus prototype. No measured effect. Maps data to evidence and frames to hypotheses, so it covers only the hypothesis kind of frame, not stories or scripts.
agent_relevance: The cleanest code-level reading of the theory found. It fits our rule: the program holds the score and the threshold, and a failed threshold is the signal for elaborate or seek-a-frame. Reframe (replace the whole hypothesis set) is only implicit.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making (mixed-initiative design)
finding: Argues that most AI decision aids fix one data-frame pair and so hide alternatives. Their fix lets either party edit evidence, add or drop hypotheses, and change evidence weights, and tags evidence as confirmed or unverified.
numbers: Interface has an evidence view and a hypotheses view, with supporting and contradicting evidence per hypothesis. Hypothesis set built by conformal prediction. Concept bottleneck model lets the user edit concepts and so change the prediction.
limits: Not tested. Anchoring on key data is asserted from Klein et al. (2007), not measured here.
agent_relevance: Supports a schema slot that stores each frame with its supporting and contradicting evidence kept apart, plus a verified flag. The program can check it, and it blocks silent explaining-away.

source: Kornowicz (2024) An Empirical Examination of the Evaluative AI Framework
finding: First direct behavioural test of Miller's evaluative AI, which is built on data-frame theory. Showing pro and con evidence for hypotheses without a recommendation did not improve decisions over no AI, and users engaged with the evidence only a little.
numbers: Online between-subjects, 5 groups, 375 analysed of 439 recruited (21 failed checks, 42 withdrew, 1 dropped). Group sizes: 62 control, 77 recommendation only, 64 evidence only, 81 both, 91 evaluative AI. Brier score (lower is better; random 0.25; the AI model itself 0.178): recommendation only 0.173, evidence only 0.185, control 0.200, both 0.201, evaluative AI 0.230. Kruskal-Wallis p=0.154, so H1 rejected. Decision time: evaluative AI 51.7 s vs recommendation only 41.2 s and control 41.3 s.
limits: One task: income above or below the median from 20 features, laypeople, logistic regression as the AI. Contradicts Le et al. 2024a, who found gains on a house-price task. The author says task and incentives differ.
agent_relevance: A caution. Showing alternatives is not enough; any gain needs the evidence to be used. Our program should force the compare step with a check, not just display rival frames.

source: Le et al. (2024a) evaluative AI vs recommendation-driven decision support, as reported in Kornowicz (2024)
finding: Reported by Kornowicz as finding that a hypothesis-driven display improved decision quality without more time, and that participants engaged with the evidence.
numbers: No figures given in the page I read.
limits: Second-hand. Task was a subjective house-price class from six features; low-level evidence was shown by default, which Kornowicz says may anchor.
agent_relevance: Set against c03: gains depend on task and on whether evidence is shown by default. Treat the benefit as unproven.

source: Jain (2025) Collaborative Causal Sensemaking: Closing the Complementarity Gap in Human-AI Decision Support
finding: Argues that LLM agents are trained as answer engines, not sensemaking partners. Proposes a loop of discrepancy, joint hypothesis, repair, action, with an explicit editable causal model as shared state and an episodic memory of past sensemaking triples.
numbers: No experiments. Cites reports that human-AI teams often do worse than the best single agent and that preference tuning gives sycophancy. Proposes local alignment that tracks only the active entities and goals.
limits: Research agenda only. Its claims about complementarity and sycophancy are cited, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Names the loop our schema needs: a discrepancy triggers a hypothesis, then a test, then repair of the stored model. It also warns that agreeing with the user's frame is the default failure, which matches guardrail G5 on conformity.

source: Yuan, Han, Ling, Ruan (2026) What Did They Mean? How LLMs Resolve Ambiguous Social Situations across Perspectives and Roles
finding: Given interpersonal scenarios with no verifiable answer, GPT-4o, Claude Opus and Gemini Flash almost never held the ambiguity open. They settled on one story, often with hedge words on top.
numbers: 24 prompts x 3 models = 72 responses. Only 9 (12.5%) kept ambiguity open. Narrative closure 29/72 (40%). Normative advice that presupposes a reading 63/72 (87.5%): Gemini 24/24, GPT 23/24, Claude 16/24. False epistemic signalling (hedges but one conclusion) 63/72; Claude 22/24 (92%). First-person framing gave alignment with the user 13/36 (36%) vs 7/36 (19%) in third person; reversal 3/36 vs 6/36.
limits: Qualitative, one coder, no agreement score, single turn, March 2025 API versions, tiny sample. The authors say the data is too small to claim bias toward authority.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the preserve side of the theory: models close early and stay closed. The program should count live competing frames and refuse a final answer on one frame while a check is still open.

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
finding: Five frontier LLMs choose an answer even when the correct option has been removed. A safety prompt that says to abstain, ask, or escalate cuts this a lot but not to zero.
numbers: MedQA 500 items (250 intact, 250 with the correct option removed) and AfriMed-QA 490 (245/245). Baseline false action about 70% on both; with the safety prompt about 48% on both. Excluding Grok 3, intact-item accuracy fell about 1.0 point. HealthBench subset n=861: baseline closure 20.7% (GPT-5.4) to 44.6% (DeepSeek R1). Safety prompt cut overall closure 4.2 to 7.9 points. Adversarial set n=191: closure 59.3% (Claude Opus 4.7) to 91.4% (DeepSeek R1). Gemini 2.5 Pro least prompt-sensitive: 55% to 48% on MedQA.
limits: Closure defined by the authors' rubric and an LLM judge. Grok 3 overcorrected and lost accuracy on answerable items. Prompt effect is model-dependent.
agent_relevance: A prompt alone leaves roughly half the failures. Supports a program-side gate: before commit, a code check that the frame set can still be falsified, with abstain as an allowed output.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning
finding: In a three-round hematologic oncology task where models must ask for data, they show anchoring and premature closure like novice clinicians. Wrong early frames mostly stayed wrong.
numbers: 32 frontier models, 20 cases, 3 rounds. Best accuracy 68.1% (Claude Opus 4.6), mean 56.3 +/- 7.4, worst 40.2%. Differential reasoning was the weakest component for all 32 (mean 43.6%) vs diagnosis 66.6%. Information utilisation predicted accuracy (R=0.69, P<0.001) and fell from 56.8% in round 1 to 25.7% in round 3. Of 323 pairs with a wrong or partial round-1 diagnosis, 212 (65.6%) stayed wrong (recovery 34.4%). Of 307 right round-1 diagnoses, 156 (50.8%) turned wrong. Reasoning rubric: 91.1% scored at least 6, yet decorrelated from accuracy. 93 error annotations on 17 models; anchoring was the most frequent bias.
limits: Judged by an LLM checked against one hematologist. Error taxonomy comes from a small annotated subset. One clinical domain, preprint.
agent_relevance: Best fit for the question about preserve. Anchoring on the first frame, low recovery, and good-looking reasoning that does not track truth. Matches G10: do not trust the reasoning text; trigger a reframe from the check result, not from the model's own rationale.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When facts arrive one piece at a time, 15 LLMs commit early to an assumed reading and then lean on their own earlier attempt. They do not recover. The loss is mostly unreliability, not aptitude.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations, 6 tasks, 15 models. Average drop 39% from single turn; 90% single turn vs 65% multi-turn in the main text. Aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%. Later first attempt helps: average score 30.9 when the first answer comes in the first 20% of the conversation vs 64.4 when it comes in the last 20%. Reasoning models o3 and DeepSeek-R1 degrade the same way; their answers are about 33% longer. Final answers in sharded runs were 20-300% longer than the first attempts.
limits: Simulated user; generation tasks (code, SQL, math, API actions, data-to-text, summaries), not diagnosis. The late-attempt result is correlational.
agent_relevance: A strong match to the preserve activity: the model builds a frame on partial data and then elaborates it. Fixes that work are structural (restate all data each turn, delay the first full answer), which a program can do.

source: Laban et al. (2025) recap, snowball and temperature checks
finding: Agent-style repetition of earlier user facts reduces the loss but does not remove it. Setting temperature to zero does not fix the unreliability.
numbers: Snowball (repeat all earlier facts each turn) mitigates 15-20% of the full-to-sharded drop (GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, 4 tasks). Recap on the last turn does better but needs knowing which turn is last.
limits: Two models in the mitigation test.
agent_relevance: A concrete scaffold move: re-send the full data list every step instead of relying on the model's memory of its frame.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: On the Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game, 11 LLMs mostly test cases that fit their current guess. More disconfirming tests go with more success.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% (45-turn limit), 80 test episodes per model-variant. Qwen3-8B baseline success 6% non-thinking, 21% thinking; Qwen3-32B 33% vs 41%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 73%. Thinking mode raised success but did not consistently raise the disconfirming ratio. The disconfirming ratio correlated positively with success in both thinking and non-thinking groups. Interventions raised average rule discovery from 42% to 56%.
limits: Numbers and rules are synthetic. Judge is an LLM. Interventions help thinking models significantly; for non-thinking models results are mixed (Dual-Goal lowered accuracy slightly).
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable test of the question-the-frame move: log the share of tests that could fail the current hypothesis. That ratio is countable in code.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Think-in-Opposites and Dual-Goal prompts, per-model results
finding: Two human debiasing prompts were tested. Think-in-Opposites: pick one feature of the last test and test its opposite. Dual-Goal: state the rule and its complement.
numbers: Think-in-Opposites raised success in all 11 model-variant settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Both raised the disconfirming ratio in 18 of 22 cases. Examples: Qwen3-32B thinking 41% to about 60%, Qwen3-8B thinking 21% to about 36-40%, Llama-3.3-70B 21% to 38%, QwQ-32B 50% to 58%. Tokens per turn rose about 1.4x for Qwen3-32B thinking (1030 to 1450).
limits: Gains significant for thinking models only. Table text in the PDF was garbled in places, so some cells are approximate.
agent_relevance: A cheap compare-with-complement move that fits an operator slot. Fire it only on the impasse signal (G1), because it costs tokens.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Distilling the debiasing behaviour and transfer to the Blicket test
finding: Fine-tuning on Think-in-Opposites traces lifted success and the disconfirming ratio, and the effect carried over to a causal Blicket task.
numbers: 72,000 training examples (1,600 episodes x 45 turns). Qwen3-8B: 0.21 base, 0.35 self-distilled with TiO, 0.44 distilled from the 32B teacher, 0.59 from the 32B teacher plus TiO (almost triple). Qwen3-32B thinking 0.41 to 0.64 after self-distillation with TiO.
limits: We do not train. Transfer shown on one new task only.
agent_relevance: Shows the behaviour is learnable. For us the same behaviour has to come from the scaffold, so treat these as a ceiling for what prompting alone might reach.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: A WordNet-based version of the 2-4-6 game with 12 LLMs. Negative testing (trying things outside the current hypothesis) is the main driver of success, and reasoning models do better.
numbers: Success: best instruction-tuned model DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33 to 35%; reasoning models GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%; small ones GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Conclusive-falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%. Share of positive tests vs falsification rate: Spearman -0.937, p<0.001 across 12 models. Hypotheses narrower than the true rule in over 50% of turns for almost all models.
limits: Fit judged by an LLM oracle backed by WordNet; oracle agreement 85 to 95% for the larger models. One game family.
agent_relevance: The strongest evidence that test choice, not knowledge, separates models. It also shows the common case is a frame that is too narrow, which calls for a broaden-the-frame move, different from replacing the frame.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) positive test strategy, as described in Bertolazzi et al. (2026)
finding: Positive testing can falsify a hypothesis when it is broader than the true rule, but cannot when it is narrower. Only negative tests can then reveal the miss.
numbers: Table 1 of Bertolazzi lists the set relations between hypothesis H and rule R and which test type falsifies.
limits: Second-hand. The original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A code rule: choose the test type from the relation between the current frame and the evidence so far, not from a fixed habit.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) multi-turn 2-4-6 benchmark, as described in Jhaveri et al. (2026)
finding: An earlier small LLM adaptation of the rule-discovery game found weak performance.
numbers: N=50 episodes, at best 26% task success.
limits: Second-hand, older models.
agent_relevance: Shows the weakness predates the newer models; the 2026 numbers show reasoning models narrowing it.

source: Wason (1960) 2-4-6 study, as summarised in Jhaveri et al. (2026)
finding: Humans on the same task: those who announced the right rule first tried more disconfirming tests.
numbers: 29 participants; 6/29 right on the first announcement; 21/29 eventually right. Mean incompatible:compatible ratio 1.79 for first-time-right vs 0.24 for first-wrong.
limits: Second-hand summary of a classic, not opened.
agent_relevance: Human baseline for the LLM results: models and people share the pattern, so the same debias moves may transfer.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an outside signal, asking a model to review and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts. Gains reported in earlier work came from oracle labels telling the model when it was wrong.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5. Without them, GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5, then 89.0; GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0; Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5, then 36.5. Multi-agent debate no better than self-consistency at equal response count.
limits: Reasoning tasks with known answers; later trained reasoners may differ. Frame choice is tested only indirectly.
agent_relevance: Backs G1 and G2: a reframe fired by the model's own doubt is unsafe; fire it from an external failed check.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o answers shift with a planted numeric hint, and four simple fixes did not remove it. One fix helped partly: show hints from both sides of the true value.
numbers: Fixes tried: chain of thought, thoughts of principles, telling the model to ignore the anchor, reflection. None gave a significant improvement. The both-anchor prompt brought GPT-4 close to the bias-free value on 8 of the 15 questions shown (those whose two hints bracketed the truth).
limits: Small school-run study, about 15 questions, few statistics, no sample sizes in the page I read. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Suggests an operator: when a frame is offered, also supply the rival frame, rather than asking the model to ignore the first. This is the compare move.

source: Qi, Lee, Breazeal, Park (2025) Does Reasoning with LLMs Improve Recognizing, Generating and Reframing Unhelpful Thoughts?
finding: On cognitive reframing (a cousin of frame change), a prompt that makes the model separate facts from interpretations beat the reasoning models. Generic chain of thought did not help.
numbers: PatternReframe, 1,000 examples (100 per distortion type). Recognition accuracy: GPT-3.5 0.425; GPT-3.5 + CoT 0.395; + self-consistency 0.419; + tree of thought 0.434; o1 0.560; Llama-3.3 0.558; GPT-4o 0.597; GPT-3.5 + Diagnosis of Thought 0.956. For free-text reframing, differences were small (ROUGE about 0.13 to 0.31) and o1 scored lowest.
limits: Therapy-style short texts, automatic text-overlap scores for generation, not outcomes. Diagnosis of Thought was designed for exactly this recognition task.
agent_relevance: A data-versus-frame split prompt (what is observed vs what is inferred) was the single large gain. Fits a program slot that extracts data items before any frame is applied.

source: Del and Fishel (2023) True Detective: A Deep Abductive Reasoning Benchmark Undoable for GPT-3 and Challenging for GPT-4
finding: Long detective puzzles show the gap between holding clues and finding the frame that explains them. With the author's solution trace supplied, GPT-4 jumps to near the best humans.
numbers: 191 puzzles, mean 1,204 words, 4 to 5 options. Human average 47%, top-10 humans 80 to 90%, random about 24%. Vanilla: GPT-3.5 0.28 / 0.26, GPT-4 0.27. Chain of thought: GPT-3.5 0.26 / 0.29, GPT-4 0.38. With the golden reasoning: GPT-3.5 0.46 / 0.63, GPT-4 0.83. GPT-4 difficulty tracks human difficulty.
limits: 2022-23 models, now old. The golden trace gives away the story, so it measures only the final inference. Human solve rates are from a website, first try only.
agent_relevance: Splits two skills: finding the explanatory frame (weak) and applying it (strong). Most gain would come from a generate-and-test frame step, not more final reasoning.

source: Dammu, Palkhiwala, Roosta, Shah (2026) iAgentBench: Benchmarking Sensemaking Capabilities of Information-Seeking Agents
finding: A benchmark of questions that need combining themes across retrieved sources. Retrieval helps, but a gap stays, and a reflect-and-retry loop helps some models and hurts others.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on iAgentBench: base 0.584, with retrieval 0.648, with reflection 0.682 (gains +0.064, +0.034). On SimpleQA the same model went 0.240, 0.740, 0.716 (reflection -0.024).
limits: Questions and judges are LLM-generated; few models. Uses sensemaking in the GraphRAG sense, not the data-frame sense.
agent_relevance: Evidence that reflection loops are unreliable (agrees with the self-correction result). Not a test of frame theory.

source: Tang, Abulikemu, Krokos, Whitley, Wang, North (2025) Agentic Reasoning and Refinement through Semantic Interaction (VIS-ReAct)
finding: A two-agent ReAct-style loop that reads a change in an analyst's visual workspace (highlight, note, cluster) and rewrites only the affected part of a sensemaking report. One agent infers intent and plans, the second edits.
numbers: Case study only; three methods compared: plain regeneration, VIS-Act (direct), VIS-ReAct (analyse, then refine). VIS-ReAct reported best on targeted change, semantic fidelity and transparency. No quantitative results found in the parts I read.
limits: Case study, no user study or sample. I read the abstract, introduction and method, not the full evaluation.
agent_relevance: A working example of a data-frame loop inside an LLM agent: the analyst edit is the new datum, the report is the frame, and only the touched part is revised. Same shape as revise only from real output (G2).

source: Mooney, Kim, Lee, Kang (2026) Structure Liberates: How Constrained Sensemaking Produces More Novel Research Output
finding: Forcing LLM ideation through eight Pirolli-Card sensemaking stages and distilling 120K such trajectories gave outputs that were more varied and better, not less. Training on trajectories that reconstruct a known paper beat open-ended foresight.
numbers: SciSense-Traj has 120,000 trajectories split evenly between Hindsight and Foresight (test 5K + 5K); models 3B to 70B across eight families. Hindsight-trained models gained 2.0% trajectory quality over Foresight-trained and had the highest diversity on every automatic metric. Coding-agent artifacts scored higher on executability, grounding and utility. Judge checked against 3 human annotators (agreement about 0.70).
limits: Pirolli and Card model, not Klein's. Quality judged by an LLM; novelty by embedding similarity. Trained models, not prompting.
agent_relevance: Closest to a staged sensemaking scaffold inside an LLM pipeline with numbers. The gain is modest (2.0%), so keep only stages that pay for themselves (G7).

source: Pirolli and Card (2005) sensemaking process, as used in Mooney et al. (2026)
finding: Eight-stage sensemaking loop used as the structure for ideation, from surveying cited work to forming and refining hypotheses.
numbers: Stage list is in Table 1 of Mooney et al.; not reproduced here.
limits: Second-hand. A sibling theory of data-frame, with a foraging loop and a sensemaking loop.
agent_relevance: Offers a stage template to compare with the frame activities; link to the foraging subfield.

source: Yuan et al. (2026) What Did They Mean? narrator and domain effects
finding: The wording of the same case changes how the model closes it, so the frame is set by how the prompt is told.
numbers: Teacher-student first-person alignment 4/9 (44%) vs third-person 0/9; friendship 33% vs 0%. Early romance had the highest alignment, 10/18 (56%), vs 4/18 teacher, 3/18 workplace, 3/18 friendship.
limits: Cells of 9 responses. Exploratory only.
agent_relevance: Retelling the case in neutral third person is a cheap reframe operator, and the two answers can be compared in code.

source: Kornowicz (2024) evaluative AI, user-reported process
finding: Users in the evidence-showing groups mentioned fewer data features in their own words than controls, which suggests that a display of evidence shifts attention.
numbers: Mentioned at least one feature: control 91.93%; recommendation only 66.23%; evaluative AI 54.95%. Mentioned the AI: recommendation only 37.66%, evidence only 50%, both 53.09%, evaluative AI 50.55% (differences not significant).
limits: Free-text self report, coded; online study.
agent_relevance: Shows how frames compete with data for attention; argues again for the program to hold the data list, not the model.

source: Braitsch et al. (2026) recovery from a wrong first frame by model
finding: Some models recover from a wrong first frame and some do not, and models with the highest recovery also had fewer initial errors.
numbers: Deterioration of right diagnoses: GPT-5.2 Reasoning 18.2% (2 of 11), Qwen3 Next 80b 83.3% (5 of 6). Recovery: Claude Opus 4.6 7 of 8 (87.5%), Qwen3 Next 80b 1 of 14 (7.1%), one model 100%.
limits: Small per-model counts.
agent_relevance: Frame revision ability varies by model, so the scaffold should measure it per model and spend more on weak ones (G12).

source: Handler, Bedi, Shah (2026) closure in underspecified vs urgent cases
finding: Models close prematurely most when the case is underspecified and looks harmless, and do better when danger cues are explicit.
numbers: Underspecified low-risk: 73.2% (GPT-5.4) to 96.1% (DeepSeek R1) closure at baseline; underspecified urgent 5.0% to 35.8%. Grok 3 urgent: 19.6% to 6.1% with the safety prompt; Claude Opus 4.7 12.3% to 4.5%. Sufficient-context control: clarification or escalation rate 3.5% in both conditions.
limits: Rubrics are physician-written; closure judged by a model.
agent_relevance: The trigger for seek-a-frame should be a missing-information signal the program can compute, not a danger cue the model has to notice.
